Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Representation Convergence: Mutual Distillation is Secretly a Form of Regularization
papers.research_question: What hinders reinforcement learning agents from generalizing like humans? How can we enable them to learn robust representations that drive human-like generalization behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies acts as an implicit regularization by improving policy robustness to irrelevant features, which leads to better generalization performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mutual distillation is a form of implicit regularization that improves generalization in reinforcement learning by enhancing policy robustness to irrelevant features and promoting invariant representations.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, improving policy robustness to irrelevant features enhances generalization performance.
Empirically, mutual distillation (DML) improves generalization performance across Procgen environments.
DML leads to more robust representations that are invariant to irrelevant features, as visualized by t-SNE.
The proposed MDPO algorithm consistently outperforms the PPO baseline in generalization.
Ablation studies indicate the improvement is due to regularization against irrelevant features, not merely additional information sharing.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we argue that mutual distillation between reinforcement learning policies serves as an implicit regularization, preventing them from overfitting to irrelevant features. We highlight two separate contributions: (i) Theoretically, for the first time, we prove that enhancing the policy robustness to irrelevant features leads to improved generalization performance. (ii) Empirically, we demonstrate that mutual distillation between policies contributes to such robustness, enabling the spontaneous emergence of invariant representations over pixel inputs. Ultimately, we do not claim to achieve state-of-the-art performance but rather focus on uncovering the underlying principles of generalization and deepening our understanding of its mechanisms.

papers.title: Neural Function Modules with Sparse Arguments: A Dynamic Approach to Integrating Information across Layers
papers.research_question: Can a neural network module that dynamically selects sparse arguments from previous layers using attention improve performance across classification, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Function Modules (NFM), a method that allows neural network layers to dynamically attend to sparse arguments from previous layers, improving performance in classification, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning.
papers.conclusion: NFM introduces a flexible architecture that allows layers to dynamically select sparse arguments, leading to improved performance across classification, generative modeling, and reinforcement learning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
NFM improves classification accuracy on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-Imagenet, and ImageNet.
NFM improves GAN performance on CIFAR-10 and Tiny-Imagenet, as measured by FID and Inception Score.
NFM improves generalization in stacked MNIST task when the number of digits differs between training and test.
NFM improves relational reasoning accuracy on Sort-of-CLEVR, especially in out-of-distribution settings.
NFM improves game scores in Atari reinforcement learning tasks.
future_direction: Integrating NFM with transformers
papers.abstract: Feed-forward neural networks consist of a sequence of layers, in which each layer performs some processing on the information from the previous layer. A downside to this approach is that each layer (or module, as multiple modules can operate in parallel) is tasked with processing the entire hidden state, rather than a particular part of the state which is most relevant for that module. Methods which only operate on a small number of input variables are an essential part of most programming languages, and they allow for improved modularity and code re-usability. Our proposed method, Neural Function Modules (NFM), aims to introduce the same structural capability into deep learning. Most of the work in the context of feed-forward networks combining top-down and bottom-up feedback is limited to classification problems. The key contribution of our work is to combine attention, sparsity, top-down and bottom-up feedback, in a flexible algorithm which, as we show, improves the results in standard classification, out-of-domain generalization, generative modeling, and learning representations in the context of reinforcement learning.

papers.title: Emergent temporal abstractions in autoregressive models enable hierarchical reinforcement learning
papers.research_question: How can we overcome inefficient learning in autoregressive models with sparse rewards by acting and exploring within internal representations to discover temporally-abstract actions for hierarchical reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that autoregressive models develop temporally-abstract action representations in their residual stream, and introduces internal RL, a method that performs reinforcement learning directly within the residual stream to achieve efficient hierarchical RL in sparse reward tasks.
papers.conclusion: Internal RL, which performs reinforcement learning directly within the residual stream of autoregressive models, enables efficient hierarchical RL by leveraging discovered temporally-abstract actions, offering a promising approach for foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Next-action predictors inherently develop temporally-abstract action representations in their residual stream.
A linear residual stream controller near mid-depth suffices to turn the sequence model into a closed-loop goal-optimizing policy capable of executing long-horizon plans.
Residual stream controller sequencing enables compositional generalization, yielding agents that combine multiple goals in ways not seen during training.
The metacontroller neural architecture discovers temporally-abstract actions without supervision by reading from and writing to the residual stream of a pretrained autoregressive model.
Internal RL, performing RL directly within the residual stream, significantly outperforms standard RL finetuning and prior hierarchical RL methods in hierarchically-structured tasks.
papers.abstract: Large-scale autoregressive models pretrained on next-token prediction and finetuned with reinforcement learning (RL) have achieved unprecedented success on many problem domains. During RL, these models explore by generating new outputs, one token at a time. However, sampling actions token-by-token can result in highly inefficient learning, particularly when rewards are sparse. Here, we show that it is possible to overcome this problem by acting and exploring within the internal representations of an autoregressive model. Specifically, to discover temporally-abstract actions, we introduce a higher-order, non-causal sequence model whose outputs control the residual stream activations of a base autoregressive model. On grid world and MuJoCo-based tasks with hierarchical structure, we find that the higher-order model learns to compress long activation sequence chunks onto internal controllers. Critically, each controller executes a sequence of behaviorally meaningful actions that unfold over long timescales and are accompanied with a learned termination condition, such that composing multiple controllers over time leads to efficient exploration on novel tasks. We show that direct internal controller reinforcement, a process we term "internal RL", enables learning from sparse rewards in cases where standard RL finetuning fails. Our results demonstrate the benefits of latent action generation and reinforcement in autoregressive models, suggesting internal RL as a promising avenue for realizing hierarchical RL within foundation models.

papers.title: Compositional Concept-Based Neuron-Level Interpretability for Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How can we provide fine-grained, neuron-level interpretability for deep reinforcement learning models by matching neuron activations with compositional concepts defined over the state space?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a concept-based neuron-level interpretation method for DRL that matches neuron activations with compositional concepts defined over the state space, enabling fine-grained explanations of individual neurons.
papers.conclusion: The proposed concept-based neuron-level interpretation method effectively reveals how individual neurons in DRL models encode meaningful, human-interpretable concepts, and its reliability is validated through targeted perturbation experiments showing consistent relationships between concept satisfaction, neuron activation, and action selection.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies interpretable neurons corresponding to human-understandable concepts in LunarLander and Blackjack environments.
In LunarLander, neurons encode concepts related to position, velocity, attitude, and contact, forming a hierarchical control structure.
In Blackjack, neurons encode strategic concepts such as high sums, low sums, and dealer's strong cards, aligning with basic Blackjack strategy.
Targeted perturbation experiments validate the interpretations by showing that violating a neuron's concept leads to predictable changes in activation and action selection.
The method works consistently across discrete and continuous action spaces (DQN and PPO).
papers.limitation: The method requires manual design of atomic concepts.
future_direction: Developing automated methods for concept identification
Exploring applications in network pruning and robustness enhancement
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL), through learning policies or values represented by neural networks, has successfully addressed many complex control problems. However, the neural networks introduced by DRL lack interpretability and transparency. Current DRL interpretability methods largely treat neural networks as black boxes, with few approaches delving into the internal mechanisms of policy/value networks. This limitation undermines trust in both the neural network models that represent policies and the explanations derived from them. In this work, we propose a novel concept-based interpretability method that provides fine-grained explanations of DRL models at the neuron level. Our method formalizes atomic concepts as binary functions over the state space and constructs complex concepts through logical operations. By analyzing the correspondence between neuron activations and concept functions, we establish interpretable explanations for individual neurons in policy/value networks. Experimental results on both continuous control tasks and discrete decision-making environments demonstrate that our method can effectively identify meaningful concepts that align with human understanding while faithfully reflecting the network's decision-making logic.

papers.title: Frustratingly Easy Regularization on Representation Can Boost Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: What is the inherent representation property of the Q-network and its target in deep reinforcement learning, and how can maintaining a distinguishable representation property improve performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes PEER, a simple regularization method that maintains a distinguishable representation property between the Q-network and its target, which improves the performance and sample efficiency of deep reinforcement learning agents.
papers.conclusion: PEER is an effective regularization method that boosts deep reinforcement learning by maintaining a distinguishable representation property, leading to improved performance and sample efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, there exists a distinguishable representation property between the representation of the Q-network and its target, with an upper bound on their similarity.
Empirically, some DRL agents (e.g., CURL) violate this property, leading to sub-optimal performance.
PEER regularization enforces the distinguishable representation property and improves performance across multiple environments and backbone algorithms.
PEER achieves state-of-the-art performance on PyBullet, DMControl, and Atari suites.
PEER is easy to implement, requiring only one line of code, and has a convergence guarantee.
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) gives the promise that an agent learns good policy from high-dimensional information, whereas representation learning removes irrelevant and redundant information and retains pertinent information. In this work, we demonstrate that the learned representation of the $Q$-network and its target $Q$-network should, in theory, satisfy a favorable distinguishable representation property. Specifically, there exists an upper bound on the representation similarity of the value functions of two adjacent time steps in a typical DRL setting. However, through illustrative experiments, we show that the learned DRL agent may violate this property and lead to a sub-optimal policy. Therefore, we propose a simple yet effective regularizer called Policy Evaluation with Easy Regularization on Representation (PEER), which aims to maintain the distinguishable representation property via explicit regularization on internal representations. And we provide the convergence rate guarantee of PEER. Implementing PEER requires only one line of code. Our experiments demonstrate that incorporating PEER into DRL can significantly improve performance and sample efficiency. Comprehensive experiments show that PEER achieves state-of-the-art performance on all 4 environments on PyBullet, 9 out of 12 tasks on DMControl, and 19 out of 26 games on Atari. To the best of our knowledge, PEER is the first work to study the inherent representation property of Q-network and its target. Our code is available at https://sites.google.com/view/peer-cvpr2023/.

papers.title: Analyzing the Hidden Activations of Deep Policy Networks: Why Representation Matters
papers.research_question: Is it possible to know a priori if a state representation will lead to fast learning in deep reinforcement learning agents, and how do neural network policies organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training?
papers.core_contribution: Pre-learned latent representations accelerate policy learning by providing an innately organized internal representation, and a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for good policy learning.
papers.conclusion: Learning a well-organized internal representation is a prerequisite for effective policy learning, and using pre-learned latent representations can remove this burden, leading to accelerated training.
papers.key_findings:
Agents trained on latent representations learn significantly faster than those trained on raw pixel images.
The internal representation of policies using latent codes is organized around task rewards even before training begins.
A poor initial representation (e.g., raw pixels in a complex task) can cause an unrecoverable collapse in the policy network's internal representation.
The organization of the internal representation evolves during training and correlates with learning progress.
The innate organization provided by latent representations is robust to different weight initialization schemes.
papers.abstract: We analyze the hidden activations of neural network policies of deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents and show, empirically, that it's possible to know a priori if a state representation will lend itself to fast learning. RL agents in high-dimensional states have two main learning burdens: (1) to learn an action-selection policy and (2) to learn to discern between useful and non-useful information in a given state. By learning a latent representation of these high-dimensional states with an auxiliary model, the latter burden is effectively removed, thereby leading to accelerated training progress. We examine this phenomenon across tasks in the PyBullet Kuka environment, where an agent must learn to control a robotic gripper to pick up an object. Our analysis reveals how neural network policies learn to organize their internal representation of the state space throughout training. The results from this analysis provide three main insights into how deep RL agents learn. First, a well-organized internal representation within the policy network is a prerequisite to learning good action-selection. Second, a poor initial representation can cause an unrecoverable collapse within a policy network. Third, a good initial representation allows an agent's policy network to organize its internal representation even before any training begins.

papers.title: Emergent mechanisms of evidence integration in recurrent neural networks
papers.research_question: How do recurrent neural networks integrate noisy sensory information over time, and do they develop behavioral and neural mechanisms similar to those found in humans and non-human primates?
papers.core_contribution: A recurrent neural network trained with reinforcement learning can learn to integrate noisy sensory evidence over time, developing behavioral and neural mechanisms similar to those found in primates, including adaptive decision timing and speed-accuracy trade-offs.
papers.conclusion: Recurrent neural networks can develop mechanisms for evidence integration that resemble those in biological systems, providing a useful tool for neuroscience to study perceptual decision making.
papers.key_findings:
The network integrates information over time when noise is dynamic, but not when noise is static.
Through reinforcement learning, the network learns to adaptively choose the number of observations needed for classification, with more observations for noisier stimuli.
The network generalizes its decision mechanism to noise levels not seen during training.
Hidden unit activities cluster into groups that encode evidence for each stimulus class, fixation period, and noise level, resembling neural recordings in primates.
The network exhibits a speed-accuracy trade-off when costs are imposed on extra observations, similar to biological systems.
papers.limitation:
The network does not improve performance with static noise masks, unlike humans, possibly due to the lack of internal noise in the model.
Training recurrent neural networks can be challenging due to vanishing gradients and sensitivity to hyperparameters.
The stochastic policy of the reinforcement learning agent may not match the deterministic threshold crossing observed in the brain.
future_direction: Incorporate internal noise into the model to study its effect on integration.
Use more complex stimuli such as natural images or videos and consider convolutional recurrent networks.
Explore deterministic policies to better match neural decision thresholds.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have enabled neural networks to solve tasks humans typically perform. These networks offer an exciting new tool for neuroscience that can give us insight in the emergence of neural and behavioral mechanisms. A big gap remains though between the very deep neural networks that have risen in popularity and outperformed many existing shallow networks in the field of computer vision and the highly recurrently connected human brain. This trend towards ever-deeper architectures raises the question why the brain has not developed such an architecture. Besides wiring constraints we argue that the brain operates under different circumstances when performing object recognition, being confronted with noisy and ambiguous sensory input. The role of time in the process of object recognition is investigated, showing that a recurrent network trained through reinforcement learning is able to learn the amount of time needed to arrive at an accurate estimate of the stimulus and develops behavioral and neural mechanisms similar to those found in the human and non-human primate literature.

papers.title: Abstract representations emerge naturally in neural networks trained to perform multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How do abstract (disentangled) representations emerge in neural networks? The paper investigates whether training on multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge.
papers.core_contribution: Training neural networks on multiple tasks causes abstract (disentangled) representations to emerge, which enables few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: Abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and could be pervasive in high-level brain regions.
papers.key_findings:
Abstract representations emerge when the number of tasks (P) exceeds the number of latent variables (D).
These representations are robust to task heterogeneity, including unbalanced tasks, contextual tasks, and partial information.
Abstract representations emerge with both supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
The multi-tasking model produces abstract representations from image inputs (2D shapes and 3D chairs).
Abstract representations enable few-sample learning and generalization to novel tasks.
future_direction: Test the predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly in neural data.
Investigate abstract representations in more complex neural network architectures and tasks.
papers.abstract: Abstract Humans and other animals demonstrate a remarkable ability to generalize knowledge across distinct contexts and objects during natural behavior. We posit that this ability to generalize arises from a specific representational geometry, that we call abstract and that is referred to as disentangled in machine learning. These abstract representations have been observed in recent neurophysiological studies. However, it is unknown how they emerge. Here, using feedforward neural networks, we demonstrate that the learning of multiple tasks causes abstract representations to emerge, using both supervised and reinforcement learning. We show that these abstract representations enable few-sample learning and reliable generalization on novel tasks. We conclude that abstract representations of sensory and cognitive variables may emerge from the multiple behaviors that animals exhibit in the natural world, and, as a consequence, could be pervasive in high-level brain regions. We also make several specific predictions about which variables will be represented abstractly.

papers.title: The Evolution of Representation in Simple Cognitive Networks
papers.research_question: How are representations developed in cognitive systems, and are they necessary for intelligent behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information-theoretic measure of representation (R) and shows that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation in simple cognitive networks.
papers.conclusion: The measure R can quantify representations in any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.
papers.key_findings:
The representation measure R increases during evolutionary adaptation in both artificial neural networks and Markov brains.
Markov brains evolve to become less dependent on sensory inputs and more dependent on internal states than artificial neural networks.
Networks form representations of specific environmental features (concepts) and these representations are distributed across nodes.
Representations are formed over the lifetime of the agent, building up as the agent integrates information.
The evolved networks can be analyzed to determine which nodes represent which environmental features.
future_direction: Future investigations on what kind of system is more powerful for making intelligent decisions using representations.
papers.abstract: Representations are internal models of the environment that can provide guidance to a behaving agent, even in the absence of sensory information. It is not clear how representations are developed and whether they are necessary or even essential for intelligent behavior. We argue here that the ability to represent relevant features of the environment is the expected consequence of an adaptive process, give a formal definition of representation based on information theory, and quantify it with a measure R. To measure how R changes over time, we evolve two types of networks--an artificial neural network and a network of hidden Markov gates--to solve a categorization task using a genetic algorithm. We find that the capacity to represent increases during evolutionary adaptation and that agents form representations of their environment during their lifetime. This ability allows the agents to act on sensorial inputs in the context of their acquired representations and enables complex and context-dependent behavior. We examine which concepts (features of the environment) our networks are representing, how the representations are logically encoded in the networks, and how they form as an agent behaves to solve a task. We conclude that R should be able to quantify the representations within any cognitive system and should be predictive of an agent's long-term adaptive success.

papers.title: From Memories to Maps: Mechanisms of In-Context Reinforcement Learning in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does episodic memory serve as a computational substrate for rapid in-context reinforcement learning in transformers, and what mechanisms emerge?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained for in-context reinforcement learning develop mechanisms that use memory tokens to cache intermediate computations, enabling rapid planning without standard model-free or model-based RL algorithms.
papers.conclusion: Memory serves as a computational resource in transformers, caching computations to support flexible behavior, and these mechanisms resemble those in the brain's hippocampal-entorhinal system.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can rapidly learn to solve novel planning tasks after minimal in-context experience.
The model develops structured representations aligned with environment geometry through in-context structure learning.
Representations are aligned across environments with shared topology, indicating cross-context alignment.
The learned RL strategy is not standard model-free or model-based planning; instead, it relies on caching intermediate computations in memory tokens.
The model's representations and memory recall patterns resemble computations in the hippocampal-entorhinal system.
papers.limitation: The kernel alignment measure is imperfect for quantifying representation structure, especially in tree mazes.
papers.abstract: Humans and animals show remarkable learning efficiency, adapting to new environments with minimal experience. This capability is not well captured by standard reinforcement learning algorithms that rely on incremental value updates. Rapid adaptation likely depends on episodic memory -- the ability to retrieve specific past experiences to guide decisions in novel contexts. Transformers provide a useful setting for studying these questions because of their ability to learn rapidly in-context and because their key-value architecture resembles episodic memory systems in the brain. We train a transformer to in-context reinforcement learn in a distribution of planning tasks inspired by rodent behavior. We then characterize the learning algorithms that emerge in the model. We first find that representation learning is supported by in-context structure learning and cross-context alignment, where representations are aligned across environments with different sensory stimuli. We next demonstrate that the reinforcement learning strategies developed by the model are not interpretable as standard model-free or model-based planning. Instead, we show that in-context reinforcement learning is supported by caching intermediate computations within the model's memory tokens, which are then accessed at decision time. Overall, we find that memory may serve as a computational resource, storing both raw experience and cached computations to support flexible behavior. Furthermore, the representations developed in the model resemble computations associated with the hippocampal-entorhinal system in the brain, suggesting that our findings may be relevant for natural cognition. Taken together, our work offers a mechanistic hypothesis for the rapid adaptation that underlies in-context learning in artificial and natural settings.

papers.title: Machine versus Human Attention in Deep Reinforcement Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: 1) How similar are the visual representations learned by RL agents and humans when performing the same task? and, 2) How do similarities and differences in these learned representations explain RL agents’ performance on these tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a comparative analysis of visual attention between deep RL agents and human experts in Atari games, showing that RL attention becomes more human-like with learning and that this similarity correlates with performance, providing insights into agent failures and the impact of hyperparameters like discount factors.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that deep RL agents can develop human-like attention patterns through learning, and comparing with human attention provides valuable insights for explaining agent performance, diagnosing failures, and guiding algorithm design to close the gap with human experts.
papers.key_findings:
RL agents' attention becomes more similar to human attention during training, and this similarity correlates positively with game performance.
Choosing an intermediate discount factor (e.g., 0.9) often leads to more human-like attention and can yield better performance than the default (0.99).
Failure analysis reveals two mistake types: agents failing to attend to the right objects ('bad perception') and attending correctly but making wrong decisions ('bad policy').
RL attention generalizes poorly to unseen game states in some games due to novel objects not encountered during training.
Attention similarity metrics (CC and KL) provide a quantitative way to interpret RL agent performance and failure modes.
papers.limitation:
Human attention data only captures overt attention (gaze) and not covert attention, which may lead to an incomplete comparison.
The study is limited to the domain of Atari games and may not generalize to other tasks or environments.
future_direction: Incorporating human attention as a learning signal or constraint to improve RL agent training.
Developing adaptive discount factors or multiple planning horizons to better match human attention and performance.
Using human-RL attention comparison for state-specific diagnosis and human-in-the-loop intervention in failure states.
papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms are powerful tools for solving visuomotor decision tasks. However, the trained models are often difficult to interpret, because they are represented as end-to-end deep neural networks. In this paper, we shed light on the inner workings of such trained models by analyzing the pixels that they attend to during task execution, and comparing them with the pixels attended to by humans executing the same tasks. To this end, we investigate the following two questions that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been previously studied. 1) How similar are the visual representations learned by RL agents and humans when performing the same task? and, 2) How do similarities and differences in these learned representations explain RL agents' performance on these tasks? Specifically, we compare the saliency maps of RL agents against visual attention models of human experts when learning to play Atari games. Further, we analyze how hyperparameters of the deep RL algorithm affect the learned representations and saliency maps of the trained agents. The insights provided have the potential to inform novel algorithms for closing the performance gap between human experts and RL agents.

papers.title: Towards Biologically Plausible Deep Learning
papers.research_question: How can credit assignment in deep networks be achieved in a biologically plausible way, avoiding the implausible aspects of backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a biologically plausible learning mechanism for deep networks that interprets Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP) as stochastic gradient descent and uses a variational EM framework with target propagation for credit assignment without backpropagation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach addresses several biological implausibility issues of backpropagation and provides a promising direction for biologically plausible deep learning, with experimental validation on MNIST.
papers.key_findings:
STDP can be interpreted as stochastic gradient descent if neural dynamics push firing rates towards better objective function values.
The training procedure corresponds to variational EM with approximate inference, implemented by neural dynamics.
Targetprop (difference target propagation) can estimate gradients without backpropagation, enabling biologically plausible deep learning.
The method can learn a generative model that produces good samples on MNIST, with log-likelihood comparable to other models.
The variational EM updates with noise can be interpreted as training a denoising auto-encoder over both visible and latent variables, and iterating the associated Markov chain yields better samples.
papers.limitation:
The approach does not address the synchronization issue (the 5th implausible element of backpropagation).
More work is needed to connect in more detail with biology, including neural implementation using spikes and constraints on weight signs.
future_direction: Incorporate lateral connections to implement priors on joint distributions between nearby neurons.
Explore the replacement of MAP-based inference by MCMC-like inference with noise injection.
Apply the ideas to supervised learning and reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Neuroscientists have long criticised deep learning algorithms as incompatible with current knowledge of neurobiology. We explore more biologically plausible versions of deep representation learning, focusing here mostly on unsupervised learning but developing a learning mechanism that could account for supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. The starting point is that the basic learning rule believed to govern synaptic weight updates (Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity) arises out of a simple update rule that makes a lot of sense from a machine learning point of view and can be interpreted as gradient descent on some objective function so long as the neuronal dynamics push firing rates towards better values of the objective function (be it supervised, unsupervised, or reward-driven). The second main idea is that this corresponds to a form of the variational EM algorithm, i.e., with approximate rather than exact posteriors, implemented by neural dynamics. Another contribution of this paper is that the gradients required for updating the hidden states in the above variational interpretation can be estimated using an approximation that only requires propagating activations forward and backward, with pairs of layers learning to form a denoising auto-encoder. Finally, we extend the theory about the probabilistic interpretation of auto-encoders to justify improved sampling schemes based on the generative interpretation of denoising auto-encoders, and we validate all these ideas on generative learning tasks.

papers.title: Higher Embedding Dimension Creates a Stronger World Model for a Simple Sorting Task
papers.research_question: How does embedding dimension affect the emergence of an internal world model in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps?
papers.core_contribution: Higher embedding dimensions lead to more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations (world models) in transformers trained on a sorting task, even after task accuracy saturates at lower dimensions.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build simple, structured internal world models even in constrained reinforcement learning settings, and increased model capacity (embedding dimension) improves the quality of these internal representations beyond what is reflected by task accuracy alone.
papers.key_findings:
The last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of input tokens.
The chosen adjacent swap corresponds to the largest difference between consecutive values in the encoded global ordering.
Task accuracy saturates at relatively low embedding dimensions (around 6 for length 6 sequences), but the fidelity and robustness of the internal ordering representation continue to improve up to around dimension 30.
Higher embedding dimensions make the learned internal mechanisms more consistent across different training runs and random seeds.
Low-dimension agents can fall into a 'local greedy trap', failing to form a coherent global ordering representation, a failure mode that decreases with higher embedding dimensions.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited in scope and scale, focusing only on adjacent transposition sorting with 1-2 layer, single-head transformers, and does not explore more complex architectures or richer environments.
Computational budget restricted the ability to test broader ranges of sequence lengths or larger training runs.
future_direction: Relax the adjacency constraint to allow arbitrary in-place swaps to see if transformers discover known efficient algorithms or novel heuristics.
Introduce stochasticity into the environment (e.g., noisy token values or partial observability) to test if the ordering circuit emerges under uncertainty.
Explore hybrid training setups (e.g., supervised pre-training on optimal swaps followed by RL fine-tuning) to see if the ordering representation becomes more robust.
Introduce multi-head attention to examine if different heads specialize in complementary subproblems.
Test the robustness of the identified circuits under pruning or quantization, and apply similar analyses to structurally richer algorithmic tasks (e.g., graph algorithms).
papers.abstract: We investigate how embedding dimension affects the emergence of an internal "world model" in a transformer trained with reinforcement learning to perform bubble-sort-style adjacent swaps. Models achieve high accuracy even with very small embedding dimensions, but larger dimensions yield more faithful, consistent, and robust internal representations. In particular, higher embedding dimensions strengthen the formation of structured internal representation and lead to better interpretability. After hundreds of experiments, we observe two consistent mechanisms: (1) the last row of the attention weight matrix monotonically encodes the global ordering of tokens; and (2) the selected transposition aligns with the largest adjacent difference of these encoded values. Our results provide quantitative evidence that transformers build structured internal world models and that model size improves representation quality in addition to end performance. We release our metrics and analyses, which can be used to probe similar algorithmic tasks.

papers.title: Learning and Understanding a Disentangled Feature Representation for Hidden Parameters in Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How to learn a feature space that represents trajectories by their hidden parameter values in an unsupervised manner, and how to use this to analyze the effects of hidden parameters.
papers.core_contribution: Presents an unsupervised method to learn a disentangled feature representation for hidden parameters in RL, using a time-invariant RNN memory training algorithm and a latent bisimulation metric learning approach.
papers.conclusion: The approach successfully learns a feature representation for hidden parameters and demonstrates its utility in estimation and visualization, with potential for future extensions to more complex environments.
papers.key_findings:
The time-invariant RNN memory and latent bisimulation metric features outperform baseline world model features in hidden parameter estimation.
The learned feature space can be visualized to show clear separation by hidden parameter values.
The method can identify which state variables are most affected by hidden parameters by comparing stateful and non-stateful world models.
The world model can generate imagined trajectories for different hidden parameter values to visualize their effects.
papers.limitation:
The environments tested represent only a small subset of real-world challenges.
The method focuses on single discrete hidden parameters and does not handle multiple or continuous hidden parameters or dynamic latent variables.
future_direction: Estimating the number of hidden parameters in an environment and decoupling their individual effects.
Extending from static hidden parameters to dynamic latent variables that change at different time-scales.
Finding more effective ways to communicate hidden parameter information to human users.
papers.abstract: Hidden parameters are latent variables in reinforcement learning (RL) environments that are constant over the course of a trajectory. Understanding what, if any, hidden parameters affect a particular environment can aid both the development and appropriate usage of RL systems. We present an unsupervised method to map RL trajectories into a feature space where distance represents the relative difference in system behavior due to hidden parameters. Our approach disentangles the effects of hidden parameters by leveraging a recurrent neural network (RNN) world model as used in model-based RL. First, we alter the standard world model training algorithm to isolate the hidden parameter information in the world model memory. Then, we use a metric learning approach to map the RNN memory into a space with a distance metric approximating a bisimulation metric with respect to the hidden parameters. The resulting disentangled feature space can be used to meaningfully relate trajectories to each other and analyze the hidden parameter. We demonstrate our approach on four hidden parameters across three RL environments. Finally we present two methods to help identify and understand the effects of hidden parameters on systems.

papers.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers.research_question: Can distilling the internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) of a large teacher model into a smaller student model improve knowledge distillation compared to only using output probabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes distilling internal representations (self-attention probabilities and hidden states) in addition to output probabilities for knowledge distillation, which consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation on GLUE tasks.
papers.conclusion: Internal knowledge distillation is a more effective method for compressing large models into smaller ones than standard distillation, as it preserves the teacher's internal behavior and generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge distillation (using KL-divergence on attention and cosine similarity on hidden states) consistently outperforms standard soft-label distillation across four GLUE datasets.
The method effectively compresses the internal behavior of the teacher into the student, as evidenced by lower KL-divergence in attention patterns.
The performance gap between internal and standard distillation increases when training data size is smaller.
The student model trained with internal distillation tends to replicate the teacher's correct and incorrect predictions more closely than a student trained with standard distillation.
The proposed progressive (PID) and stacked (SID) internal distillation algorithms allow the student to learn internal representations layer-by-layer, with SID performing best when combined with soft-label distillation throughout training.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers.title: Sparse Reward Subsystem in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does there exist a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states analogous to the biological reward subsystem, and what are its properties?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sparse reward subsystem in LLM hidden states, consisting of value neurons that encode state value and dopamine neurons that encode reward prediction error, and shows their critical role in reasoning and their robustness across models and tasks.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess a sparse reward subsystem analogous to the biological reward subsystem, which is consistent across tasks, layers, model scales, and architectures, and has potential applications.
papers.key_findings:
Value neurons exist in LLM hidden states and can predict the value of the current state using only a small fraction of neurons.
Ablating even 1% of value neurons severely impairs reasoning performance, while random ablation does not.
Value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, layers, and architectural designs.
Value neurons are transferable across different datasets and across models fine-tuned from the same base model.
Dopamine neurons exist and encode reward prediction error, with activation patterns correlating with positive and negative surprises.
papers.limitation: Dopamine neurons are demonstrated primarily through case studies rather than quantitative metrics.
future_direction: Further explore applications of the reward subsystem for detecting and guiding LLM generation and reasoning.
Develop quantitative metrics for measuring dopamine neurons.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify a sparse reward subsystem within the hidden states of Large Language Models (LLMs), drawing an analogy to the biological reward subsystem in the human brain. We demonstrate that this subsystem contains value neurons that represent the model's internal expectation of state value, and through intervention experiments, we establish the importance of these neurons for reasoning. Our experiments reveal that these value neurons are robust across diverse datasets, model scales, and architectures; furthermore, they exhibit significant transferability across different datasets and models fine-tuned from the same base model. By examining cases where value predictions and actual rewards diverge, we identify dopamine neurons within the reward subsystem which encode reward prediction errors (RPE). These neurons exhibit high activation when the reward is higher than expected and low activation when the reward is lower than expected.

papers.title: Toward Explainable Offline RL: Analyzing Representations in Intrinsically Motivated Decision Transformers
papers.research_question: How does intrinsic motivation shape learned representations in Elastic Decision Transformers, and what are the cognitive mechanisms underlying performance improvements?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a post-hoc explainability framework to analyze how intrinsic motivation shapes embedding geometry in Elastic Decision Transformers, revealing that different intrinsic motivation variants create distinct representational structures (compactness vs. orthogonality) that correlate with performance in an environment-specific manner.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsic motivation in Elastic Decision Transformers shapes learned representations by acting as a representational prior, creating environment-specific organizational structures in the embedding geometry that correlate with performance improvements, providing mechanistic insights beyond simple exploration enhancement.
papers.key_findings:
Different intrinsic motivation variants create fundamentally different representational structures: EDT-SIL (operating on state embeddings) promotes compact representations, while EDT-TIL (operating on transformer outputs) enhances representational orthogonality.
Strong environment-specific correlation patterns exist between embedding metrics (covariance trace, L2 norm, cosine similarity) and task performance across locomotion tasks.
Intrinsic motivation acts as a representational prior that shapes embedding geometry in cognitively plausible ways, creating environment-specific organizational structures that facilitate better decision-making.
The 3-layer Random Network Distillation (RND) configuration emerged as optimal for both EDT-SIL and EDT-TIL variants.
Statistical analysis (ANOVA) confirms that the observed embedding differences between models are significant.
papers.limitation:
The study primarily focused on the geometrical properties of the embeddings rather than on explicit explainability measures.
The initial variations in Human-Normalized Scores (HNS) are very small (of the order of percent), which requires further testing to prove the significance of the results.
future_direction: Application of explainability models to understand the impact of certain features and vector dimensionality reduction on model performance.
Extend the framework to analyze transformer outputs and action representations, and investigate temporal dynamics of embedding evolution during training.
papers.abstract: Elastic Decision Transformers (EDTs) have proved to be particularly successful in offline reinforcement learning, offering a flexible framework that unifies sequence modeling with decision-making under uncertainty. Recent research has shown that incorporating intrinsic motivation mechanisms into EDTs improves performance across exploration tasks, yet the representational mechanisms underlying these improvements remain unexplored. In this paper, we introduce a systematic post-hoc explainability framework to analyze how intrinsic motivation shapes learned embeddings in EDTs. Through statistical analysis of embedding properties (including covariance structure, vector magnitudes, and orthogonality), we reveal that different intrinsic motivation variants create fundamentally different representational structures. Our analysis demonstrates environment-specific correlation patterns between embedding metrics and performance that explain why intrinsic motivation improves policy learning. These findings show that intrinsic motivation operates beyond simple exploration bonuses, acting as a representational prior that shapes embedding geometry in biologically plausible ways, creating environment-specific organizational structures that facilitate better decision-making.

papers.title: Circuit-Aware Reward Training: A Mechanistic Framework for Longtail Robustness in RLHF
papers.research_question: What is the role of neural circuit specialization in reward models for longtail robustness, and how can it be leveraged to prevent reward hacking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mechanistic interpretability framework to identify and mitigate longtail vulnerabilities in reward models through circuit-aware training.
papers.conclusion: Reward hacking is a mechanistic failure due to longtail circuit specialization, and CART connects mechanistic interpretability with practical alignment to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Reward models develop specialized neural circuits for processing rare preference scenarios.
Longtail generalization error is bounded by the number of specialized circuits and their divergence from common circuits.
Vulnerable circuits can be identified through activation patterns, coherence analysis, and causal validation.
Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART) uses targeted interventions like data augmentation and regularization to improve robustness.
CART provides a principled framework for connecting circuit specialization to reward model failures.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability methods are computationally intensive, raising scalability concerns.
Circuits may not always exhibit clean specialization, as networks often have overlapping or dynamic structures.
Evaluating robustness on longtail scenarios is difficult, requiring new benchmarks and protocols.
Extension to other modalities such as vision, robotics, or multimodal alignment remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities like vision and robotics.
Developing new benchmarks and protocols for evaluating longtail robustness.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) reward models exhibit systematic failures on longtail distributions, leading to reward hacking and misalignment. We propose a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies specialized neural circuits responsible for rare-event processing in reward models. Drawing from recent advances showing distributed specialization for rare tokens in language models\citep{liu2025no, liu2025emergent}, we hypothesize that reward models also develop functionally distinct circuits for longtail scenarios. Our theoretical framework establishes formal connections between circuit specialization, reward generalization bounds, and longtail performance. We introduce \textbf{Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART)}, which uses circuit analysis to guide data augmentation, regularization, and ensemble strategies. This approach provides both theoretical insights into reward model failures and practical interventions for improving longtail robustness.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Emergence of task-dependent representations in working memory circuits
papers.research_question: How do task-dependent representations emerge in working memory circuits? Specifically, can reward-dependent learning explain the variety of prefrontal cortex (PFC) representations in different working memory tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Reward-dependent learning (combining reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity and homeostatic plasticity) can explain the emergence of task-dependent representations in working memory circuits, as observed in experimental data.
papers.conclusion: Reward-dependent learning plays a critical role in shaping prefrontal cortex representations during working memory tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The model successfully learns delayed response tasks and shows neural selectivity similar to experimental observations.
In delayed categorization tasks, neurons develop category selectivity.
When learning multiple independent categorization tasks, neurons multiplex information across tasks.
When learning overlapping categorization tasks, neurons segregate into task-specific subpopulations.
Reward-dependent learning is critical for these representations; unsupervised learning leads to poorer performance and representations.
papers.limitation:
The abstract network model is simplified and does not capture all temporal dynamics of more realistic spiking neural networks.
The plasticity mechanisms (e.g., reward-dependent learning, homeostatic plasticity) are simplistic and could be refined.
future_direction: Investigate reward-dependent learning in more realistic spiking neural networks.
Refine the models of plasticity mechanisms, including inhibitory plasticity and structural plasticity.
Study the effects of neuromodulation on homeostatic plasticity.
papers.abstract: A wealth of experimental evidence suggests that working memory circuits preferentially represent information that is behaviorally relevant. Still, we are missing a mechanistic account of how these representations come about. Here we provide a simple explanation for a range of experimental findings, in light of prefrontal circuits adapting to task constraints by reward-dependent learning. In particular, we model a neural network shaped by reward-modulated spike-timing dependent plasticity (r-STDP) and homeostatic plasticity (intrinsic excitability and synaptic scaling). We show that the experimentally-observed neural representations naturally emerge in an initially unstructured circuit as it learns to solve several working memory tasks. These results point to a critical, and previously unappreciated, role for reward-dependent learning in shaping prefrontal cortex activity.

papers.title: The Interpretability of Codebooks in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning is Limited
papers.research_question: Does vector quantization provide interpretability in model-based reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: Vector quantization alone is insufficient for interpretability in model-based reinforcement learning due to inconsistent codes and lack of semantic disentanglement.
papers.conclusion: Vector quantization cannot provide interpretability of transition models in MBRL without additional constraints for semantic alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Codes are inconsistent and do not consistently associate with semantic entities.
Most heatmaps from Grad-CAM have zero values, indicating limited usefulness for interpretability.
Mean cosine similarity between code embeddings is low, similar to random crops.
Only a handful of codes show strong clustering and interpretability.
Co-occurring codes can be interpretable but are rare and limited to specific episodes.
papers.limitation:
Codes are not consistent enough to be grounded to a semantic concept.
Co-occurring codes account for a very small portion of observations, limiting interpretability.
future_direction: Deeper study of discretization characteristics to ensure semantic associations.
papers.abstract: Interpretability of deep reinforcement learning systems could assist operators with understanding how they interact with their environment. Vector quantization methods -- also called codebook methods -- discretize a neural network's latent space that is often suggested to yield emergent interpretability. We investigate whether vector quantization in fact provides interpretability in model-based reinforcement learning. Our experiments, conducted in the reinforcement learning environment Crafter, show that the codes of vector quantization models are inconsistent, have no guarantee of uniqueness, and have a limited impact on concept disentanglement, all of which are necessary traits for interpretability. We share insights on why vector quantization may be fundamentally insufficient for model interpretability.

papers.title: A framework for the emergence and analysis of language in social learning agents
papers.research_question: How are internal representations structured and optimized for communication between agents in social learning, and how does language emerge from such interactions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a teacher-student reinforcement learning framework with a sparse autoencoder to study emergent communication, showing that student feedback shapes the language embedding to prioritize policy information, improving task performance and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides insights into how language emerges from social interactions and how communication constraints shape internal representations, with implications for generalization in cooperative multi-agent systems.
papers.key_findings:
Providing teacher information to the student leads to higher task completion rates and the ability to generalize to unseen tasks.
Optimizing message content with student feedback improves information encoding, altering the latent structure to focus on policy (goal location and initial action) rather than state space (wall position).
The emergent communication exhibits properties of natural language such as compositionality (topographic similarity) and pressure towards entropy minimization.
Feeding back the student's own task information (closing-the-loop) retains some task-relevant information but results in degraded performance and loss of generalization to unknown goals.
Bi-directional communication (with feedback) is critical for transmitting helpful information and enhances the reconstruction capability of the autoencoder.
future_direction: Understanding how social agents reconcile abstractions from their own experience with those acquired through communication.
Achieving a balance between tutoring and learning in multi-task and multi-agent systems to maintain a relevant and generalizable message space.
papers.abstract: Neural systems have evolved not only to solve environmental challenges through internal representations but also, under social constraints, to communicate these to conspecifics. In this work, we aim to understand the structure of these internal representations and how they may be optimized to transmit pertinent information from one individual to another. Thus, we build on previous teacher-student communication protocols to analyze the formation of individual and shared abstractions and their impact on task performance. We use reinforcement learning in grid-world mazes where a teacher network passes a message to a student to improve task performance. This framework allows us to relate environmental variables with individual and shared representations. We compress high-dimensional task information within a low-dimensional representational space to mimic natural language features. In coherence with previous results, we find that providing teacher information to the student leads to a higher task completion rate and an ability to generalize tasks it has not seen before. Further, optimizing message content to maximize student reward improves information encoding, suggesting that an accurate representation in the space of messages requires bi-directional input. These results highlight the role of language as a common representation among agents and its implications on generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Internal knowledge representation on trainer agents by using interactive reinforcement learning
papers.research_question: What internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents determine which agent is a better advisor in interactive reinforcement learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that in interactive reinforcement learning, trainer agents with homogeneously distributed experience (polymath agents) are better advisors than those with high reward but limited knowledge (fast agents), due to more complete internal knowledge representation.
papers.conclusion: Polymath agents, with homogeneously distributed experience, have more complete internal knowledge representation and are therefore better advisors for other RL agents compared to fast agents with high reward but incomplete knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fast agents accumulate more reward but have incomplete knowledge in states not on the shortest path.
Polymath agents have homogeneously distributed experience and explore multiple paths.
Accumulating high reward does not necessarily make an agent a good trainer.
Internal Q-value heat maps reveal uniform regions in fast agents indicating no preferred action in some states.
Polymath agents have more complete internal knowledge representation and are better candidates for advisors.
papers.abstract: Interactive reinforcement learning has become an important apprenticeship approach to speed up convergence in classic reinforcement learning problems. On some occasions, the trainer may be another artificial agent which in turn was trained using reinforcement learning methods to afterward become an advisor for other learner-agents. In this work, we analyze internal representation and characteristics of artificial trainer-agents to determine which agent may outperform others to become a better advisor.

papers.title: Emergent spatial representations in reinforcement learning
papers.research_question: How do task demands, action spaces, and sensory inputs shape the emergence of egocentric and allocentric spatial representations in reinforcement learning agents?
papers.core_contribution: The work shows that sensory inputs, navigation task, and agent output (closed-loop components) shape the spatial representations that emerge in RL agents, and presents a flexible software framework (CoBeL-RL) for closed-loop modeling in neuroscience.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the complex nature of spatial representations and underlines the importance of studying them in the context of the behaviors they support.
papers.key_findings:
The choice of navigation strategy (egocentric vs allocentric) emerges from task demands.
Spatial representations (place-like vs vector-like) are modulated by both task and navigation strategy.
Sensory signals can compete or integrate to guide navigation; integration is necessary for robustness but can reduce efficiency when a single signal is sufficient.
The closed-loop interaction between behavior and representations shapes the emergent spatial representations.
The CoBeL-RL framework enables the use of RL agents for closed-loop modeling in neuroscience.
papers.abstract: Spatial navigation is a complex and fundamental problem for both biological and artificial agents. Understanding this problem has practical implications for several areas ranging from clinical diagnostics to autonomous robotics. A crucial gap in our current knowledge is how neural representations relate to experimentally observed behaviors. Here, we address this challenge from multiple perspectives. We propose a taxonomy of spatial navigation grounded in both behavioral and neural evidence, bridging these two domains. Next, we use computational modeling using reinforcement learning to understand how navigation task, action space, and sensory inputs interact to shape behavior and spatial representations. Finally, we propose a modular software framework designed to facilitate reinforcement learning based modeling of navigation and other paradigms relevant to behavioral and neuroscience research.

papers.title: Interpretable Learning Dynamics in Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How does intrinsic motivation shape attention, behavior, and representation learning in unsupervised reinforcement learning agents?
papers.core_contribution: An interpretability framework combining Grad-CAM, LRP, and VAE-based analysis to study how intrinsic motivation shapes attention, behavior, and representation learning in unsupervised RL agents.
papers.conclusion: Curiosity-driven agents develop more structured attention and representations, while value-based agents like DQN show diffuse attention and unstructured representations, highlighting the role of intrinsic motivation and architecture in interpretable RL.
papers.key_findings:
Curiosity-driven agents (ICM, RND, Transformer-RND) exhibit broader spatial attention, higher exploration coverage, and richer latent representations than extrinsically motivated agents like DQN.
Transformer-RND combines wide attention, high exploration coverage, and compact, structured latent representations.
On-policy agents (PPO, Transformer-RND) show more dynamic attention shifts over time compared to off-policy agents.
DQN, despite low exploration, can achieve competitive clustering metrics due to overfitted representations, highlighting the need for multiple evaluation methods.
The proposed metrics (attention diversity and attention change rate) effectively capture spatial and temporal patterns of agent perception.
papers.limitation: Our analysis focuses on a single environment and fixed hyperparameters.
future_direction: Extending interpretability methods to model-based and hierarchical RL agents for richer reasoning insights.
Incorporating temporal attention visualization in Transformer-based agents to interpret long-term dependencies.
Developing online tools for real-time policy debugging using saliency and latent diagnostics during training.
papers.abstract: We present an interpretability framework for unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) agents, aimed at understanding how intrinsic motivation shapes attention, behavior, and representation learning. We analyze five agents DQN, RND, ICM, PPO, and a Transformer-RND variant trained on procedurally generated environments, using Grad-CAM, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP), exploration metrics, and latent space clustering. To capture how agents perceive and adapt over time, we introduce two metrics: attention diversity, which measures the spatial breadth of focus, and attention change rate, which quantifies temporal shifts in attention. Our findings show that curiosity-driven agents display broader, more dynamic attention and exploratory behavior than their extrinsically motivated counterparts. Among them, TransformerRND combines wide attention, high exploration coverage, and compact, structured latent representations. Our results highlight the influence of architectural inductive biases and training signals on internal agent dynamics. Beyond reward-centric evaluation, the proposed framework offers diagnostic tools to probe perception and abstraction in RL agents, enabling more interpretable and generalizable behavior.

papers.title: Temporal Disentanglement of Representations for Improved Generalisation in Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve generalization in image-based reinforcement learning to unseen variations in environment variables (both relevant and irrelevant to the task) by learning disentangled representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TED, a self-supervised auxiliary task that learns disentangled representations for RL, leading to improved generalization to unseen environment variables.
papers.conclusion: TED improves generalization of RL algorithms to unseen values of environment variables and is a step toward making RL algorithms more robust for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
TED improves generalization and adaptation to unseen colors and levels in RL tasks.
TED achieves higher disentanglement scores compared to baselines.
TED outperforms state-of-the-art baselines including domain randomization in many tasks.
TED can be used with existing RL algorithms and does not require a decoder.
TED shows lower variance across seeds compared to baselines.
papers.limitation:
Guarantees of disentanglement usually assume the factors of variation are independent and do not generalize to correlated factors.
Theoretical proof for disentanglement in time-series containing both stationary and non-stationary factors is an open problem.
TED introduces a loss coefficient hyperparameter that must be tuned to the task.
future_direction: Relaxing the independence assumption for factors of variation.
Automatically tuning the loss coefficient based on the current disentanglement score.
Extending the horizon of the temporal sample to t+k with k>1.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are often unable to generalise well to environment variations in the state space that were not observed during training. This issue is especially problematic for image-based RL, where a change in just one variable, such as the background colour, can change many pixels in the image. The changed pixels can lead to drastic changes in the agent's latent representation of the image, causing the learned policy to fail. To learn more robust representations, we introduce TEmporal Disentanglement (TED), a self-supervised auxiliary task that leads to disentangled image representations exploiting the sequential nature of RL observations. We find empirically that RL algorithms utilising TED as an auxiliary task adapt more quickly to changes in environment variables with continued training compared to state-of-the-art representation learning methods. Since TED enforces a disentangled structure of the representation, our experiments also show that policies trained with TED generalise better to unseen values of variables irrelevant to the task (e.g. background colour) as well as unseen values of variables that affect the optimal policy (e.g. goal positions).

papers.title: Primate-like perceptual decision making emerges through deep recurrent reinforcement learning
papers.research_question: Does primate-like decision making emerge in artificial agents trained to maximize reward in a noisy, temporally uncertain environment?
papers.core_contribution: Deep recurrent neural networks trained with reinforcement learning on a noisy perceptual discrimination task develop primate-like decision making abilities and internal mechanisms similar to those observed in primates.
papers.conclusion: Primate-like decision making emerges from training in noisy, temporally uncertain environments, and recurrence and environmental noise are critical factors for this emergence.
papers.key_findings:
Agents display stereotyped decision making behaviors: accuracy and response times vary with coherence, and they learn speed-accuracy tradeoffs.
Internal dynamics reflect momentary and accumulated decision evidence, similar to primate MT and LIP areas.
Changes of mind can be decoded from neural dynamics, and they are more frequent in difficult trials and tend to be corrective.
Changes of mind are also observed in movement trajectories for agents controlling an arm.
The critic output of the agent correlates with confidence, matching human confidence ratings.
papers.limitation:
Agents were trained in a simplified environment compared to the real world.
Agents were trained with a simplified neural architecture compared to the primate brain.
Agents displayed low behavioral and neural variability relative to biological decision makers.
future_direction: Integrate the limitations (simplified environment, architecture, variability) into artificial agents to better understand biological solutions.
Consider more complex environments and architectures in future work.
papers.abstract: Progress has led to a detailed understanding of the neural mechanisms that underlie decision making in primates. However, less is known about why such mechanisms are present in the first place. Theory suggests that primate decision making mechanisms, and their resultant behavioral abilities, emerged to maximize reward in the face of noisy, temporally evolving information. To test this theory, we trained an end-to-end deep recurrent neural network using reinforcement learning on a noisy perceptual discrimination task. Networks learned several key abilities of primate-like decision making including trading off speed for accuracy, and flexibly changing their mind in the face of new information. Internal dynamics of these networks suggest that these abilities were supported by similar decision mechanisms as those observed in primate neurophysiological studies. These results provide experimental support for key pressures that gave rise to the primate ability to make flexible decisions.

papers.title: Hippocampal representations emerge when training recurrent neural networks on a memory dependent maze navigation task
papers.research_question: Can recurrent neural networks learn goal-directed behaviour using strategies similar to the brain, and do they develop internal representations resembling hippocampal place cells when trained with a combination of predictive sensory learning and reinforcement learning?
