The prevalence of these complex dynamics in RL is controllably modulated by weight initialization and correlates strongly with performance gains, particularly as task complexity increases. Our results establish the learning algorithm as a primary determinant of emergent computation, revealing how reward-based optimization autonomously discovers sophisticated dynamical mechanisms that are less accessible to direct gradient-based optimization. These findings provide both mechanistic insights into neural computation and actionable principles for designing adaptive AI systems.

papers.title: Disentangling Representations through Multi-task Learning
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do disentangled representations emerge in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Multi-task learning in evidence accumulation tasks leads to disentangled representations in the latent state of autoregressive models, with theoretical guarantees on emergence conditions.
papers.conclusion: Multi-task learning establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, explaining their generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical guarantees show that any optimal multi-task classifier must encode a maximum likelihood estimate of the ground truth in its latent state, leading to abstract and disentangled representations as the number of tasks increases.
RNNs trained on multi-task classification learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, enabling zero-shot out-of-distribution generalization.
Transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, achieving orthogonality even with fewer tasks compared to RNNs.
Noise in observations is necessary for disentangled representations to emerge, as it prevents saturation and preserves distance information.
The framework is robust to various manipulations including correlated inputs, non-linear decision boundaries, and free reaction-time tasks.
future_direction: Characterizing representation learning with multiple manifold decision boundaries
Exploring interplay between task diversity, energy constraints, and the emergence of shared representations
papers.abstract: Intelligent perception and interaction with the world hinges on internal representations that capture its underlying structure (''disentangled'' or ''abstract'' representations). Disentangled representations serve as world models, isolating latent factors of variation in the world along approximately orthogonal directions, thus facilitating feature-based generalization. We provide experimental and theoretical results guaranteeing the emergence of disentangled representations in agents that optimally solve multi-task evidence accumulation classification tasks, canonical in the neuroscience literature. The key conceptual finding is that, by producing accurate multi-task classification estimates, a system implicitly represents a set of coordinates specifying a disentangled representation of the underlying latent state of the data it receives. The theory provides conditions for the emergence of these representations in terms of noise, number of tasks, and evidence accumulation time. We experimentally validate these predictions in RNNs trained to multi-task, which learn disentangled representations in the form of continuous attractors, leading to zero-shot out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in predicting latent factors. We demonstrate the robustness of our framework across autoregressive architectures, decision boundary geometries and in tasks requiring classification confidence estimation. We find that transformers are particularly suited for disentangling representations, which might explain their unique world understanding abilities. Overall, our framework establishes a formal link between competence at multiple tasks and the formation of disentangled, interpretable world models in both biological and artificial systems, and helps explain why ANNs often arrive at human-interpretable concepts, and how they both may acquire exceptional zero-shot generalization capabilities.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Intrinsic Robotic Introspection: Learning Internal States From Neuron Activations
papers.research_question: How to extract abstract representations of internal states from artificial neural networks and how these representations can be used to inform the execution of a robotic manipulation task.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an introspective framework that uses a Variational Autoencoder to learn internal states from neural network activations, demonstrating that these states improve the training convergence and success rate of a behavior-based reinforcement learning agent in a robotic manipulation task.
papers.conclusion: Internal states improve the performance of BBRL by incorporating environment observation and hidden activations, enabling faster learning of the robotic task, as supported by statistical significance analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Using internal states as input to the actor-critic reduces the number of training episodes needed for convergence by about 1300 episodes.
Concatenating latent means and log variances as input results in the fastest convergence and highest success value.
Internal states improve the state values for all robotic behaviors (approach, grasp, retract).
The approach is robust to noise in the input, maintaining performance with 5% and 10% noise levels.
The latent space learned by the VAE encodes temporal transitions between behaviors, as visualized with t-SNE.
future_direction: Explore using internal states to dictate the behavior of BBRL instead of using an actor-critic.
Adopt an unsupervised learning approach to train the robot.
Explore how internal states can be evolved using evolutionary techniques to improve performance and acquire new skills.
papers.abstract: We present an introspective framework inspired by the process of how humans perform introspection. Our working assumption is that neural network activations encode information, and building internal states from these activations can improve the performance of an actor-critic model. We perform experiments where we first train a Variational Autoencoder model to reconstruct the activations of a feature extraction network and use the latent space to improve the performance of an actor-critic when deciding which low-level robotic behaviour to execute. We show that internal states reduce the number of episodes needed by about 1300 episodes while training an actor-critic, denoting faster convergence to get a high success value while completing a robotic task.

papers.title: Learning Dynamics in RL Post-Training for Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the learning dynamics of reinforcement learning post-training for language models, aiming to explain phenomena such as reduced output diversity and increased model confidence.
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the learning dynamics of RL post-training using an empirical NTK framework, explaining increased model confidence and reduced output diversity, and proposes a classifier-first reinforcement learning (CF-RL) method to accelerate optimization.
papers.conclusion: The study formalizes the learning dynamics of RL post-training, explaining increased model confidence and motivating the CF-RL method, which accelerates optimization and differs from supervised LP-FT.
papers.key_findings:
RL post-training increases model confidence and reduces output diversity due to limited variability in feature representations.
The classifier learns faster than other model parameters during RL optimization.
The proposed CF-RL method accelerates RL optimization compared to standard RL.
CF-RL does not reduce feature distortion or amplify classifier norms, unlike linear-probing-then-fine-tuning in supervised learning.
CF-RL reshapes the classifier to emphasize structural and formatting tokens rather than content-bearing tokens.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training is a critical stage in modern language model development, playing a key role in improving alignment and reasoning ability. However, several phenomena remain poorly understood, including the reduction in output diversity. To gain a broader understanding of RL post-training, we analyze the learning dynamics of RL post-training from a perspective that has been studied in supervised learning but remains underexplored in RL. We adopt an empirical neural tangent kernel (NTK) framework and decompose the NTK into two components to characterize how RL updates propagate across training samples. Our analysis reveals that limited variability in feature representations can cause RL updates to systematically increase model confidence, providing an explanation for the commonly observed reduction in output diversity after RL post-training. Furthermore, we show that effective learning in this regime depends on rapidly shaping the classifier, which directly affects the gradient component of the NTK. Motivated by these insights, we propose classifier-first reinforcement learning (CF-RL), a simple two-stage training strategy that prioritizes classifier updates before standard RL optimization. Experimental results validate our theoretical analysis by demonstrating increased model confidence and accelerated optimization under CF-RL. Additional analysis shows that the mechanism underlying CF-RL differs from that of linear-probing-then-fine-tuning in supervised learning. Overall, our study formalizes the learning dynamics of RL post-training and motivates further analysis and improvement.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: The Horcrux: Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition for Detecting and Mitigating Reward Hacking in Embodied AI Systems
papers.research_question: How can mechanistically interpretable task decomposition be used to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture that decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks and provides diagnostic visualizations to detect and mitigate reward hacking in embodied AI systems.
papers.conclusion: MITD, a hierarchical planning model with built-in interpretability, enables systematic identification of reward-hacking behaviors and demonstrates how integrating analytical hooks and visualization tools offers new perspectives for monitoring, steering, and evaluating agent strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Optimal decomposition depths of 12-25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34% across four failure modes.
Attention mechanisms exert disproportionate influence over behavior; masking or reweighting attention reduces reliance on misaligned features.
Reward hacking behaviors are concentrated in specific regions (e.g., layers 3–7) rather than distributed uniformly, suggesting avenues for targeted mitigation.
An inverted-U stability pattern emerges: reward hacking peaks at moderate decomposition depths (4–8 steps) and is minimized at 12–25 steps.
MITD provides actionable insight into the model's decision-making through interpretable visualizations like Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts.
papers.limitation:
Limited scale: 1,000 training samples, 50 held-out test samples, single model family (GPT-2).
Generalization remains uncertain; findings may not transfer to larger models (e.g., Llama, GPT-3/4/5 scale) or diverse RLHF/AI Safety datasets.
Hacking category detection relies on empirically-set thresholds chosen on validation data, risking overfitting.
Causality between decomposition depth and reduced hacking is correlational, not causal; the inverted-U pattern could reflect simple capacity bottlenecking.
Visualizations (Attention Waterfall, Pathway Flow) are post-hoc analyses; they diagnose but do not intervene in real-time.
Metric definitions (Consistency Score via executor agreement; Reward Correlation as Pearson ρ) are task-agnostic proxies and may not capture all aspects of misalignment.
future_direction: Scaling evaluation to Ntrain ≥ 10,000, Ntest ≥ 500 with stratified sampling per failure mode, and validating decomposition stability across model families (decoder-only, encoder-decoder, reasoning-scale LLMs).

Investigating whether the optimal zone [12–25] persists across architectures or is architecture-specific, and conducting ablation studies isolating contributions of Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules versus depth alone.

Conducting causal interventions—ablating specific attention heads or layer groups identified by Neural Pathway Flow—to validate that visualizations reveal actionable targets, and exploring real-time mitigation using predicted hacking risk to dynamically reweight executor outputs.
papers.abstract: Embodied AI agents exploit reward signal flaws through reward hacking, achieving high proxy scores while failing true objectives. We introduce Mechanistically Interpretable Task Decomposition (MITD), a hierarchical transformer architecture with Planner, Coordinator, and Executor modules that detects and mitigates reward hacking. MITD decomposes tasks into interpretable subtasks while generating diagnostic visualizations including Attention Waterfall Diagrams and Neural Pathway Flow Charts. Experiments on 1,000 HH-RLHF samples reveal that decomposition depths of 12 to 25 steps reduce reward hacking frequency by 34 percent across four failure modes. We present new paradigms showing that mechanistically grounded decomposition offers a more effective way to detect reward hacking than post-hoc behavioral monitoring.

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Why is Your Language Model a Poor Implicit Reward Model?
papers.research_question: Why do implicit reward models (IM-RMs) generalize worse than explicit reward models (EX-RMs), especially out-of-distribution, despite being nearly identical?
papers.core_contribution: IM-RMs rely more heavily on superficial token-level cues than EX-RMs, leading to worse generalization under token-level distribution shifts, but comparable or better performance under domain shifts.
papers.conclusion: Seemingly minor design choices in reward models (explicit vs. implicit) can have an outsized effect on their generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
IM-RMs can learn to verify without learning to generate, challenging the hypothesis that the generation-verification gap explains their poorer generalization.
The learning dynamics of IM-RMs are more sensitive to specific tokens, while EX-RMs generalize via hidden representations.
IM-RMs are less robust to token-level shifts (e.g., paraphrasing, translation) but can perform comparably or better under domain shifts (e.g., math, code).
future_direction: Further research into the implicit biases of different reward model types and enhancing their robustness.
papers.abstract: Reward models are key to language model post-training and inference pipelines. Conveniently, recent work showed that every language model defines an implicit reward model (IM-RM), without requiring any architectural changes. However, such IM-RMs tend to generalize worse, especially out-of-distribution, compared to explicit reward models (EX-RMs) that apply a dedicated linear head over the hidden representations of a language model. The existence of a generalization gap is puzzling, as EX-RMs and IM-RMs are nearly identical. They can be trained using the same data, loss function, and language model, and differ only in how the reward is computed. Toward a fundamental understanding of the implicit biases underlying different reward model types, we investigate the root cause of this gap. Our main finding, backed by theory and experiments, is that IM-RMs rely more heavily on superficial token-level cues. Consequently, they often generalize worse than EX-RMs under token-level distribution shifts, as well as in-distribution. Furthermore, we provide evidence against alternative hypotheses for the generalization gap. Most notably, we challenge the claim that IM-RMs struggle in tasks where generation is harder than verification because they can operate both as a verifier and a generator. Overall, our results highlight that seemingly minor design choices can substantially impact the generalization behavior of reward models.

papers.title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Interpretable Policy Distillation
papers.research_question: How to provide human-understandable explanations for deep reinforcement learning policies via interpretable policy distillation while maintaining high fidelity and performance?
papers.core_contribution: A unified framework for explainable reinforcement learning via interpretable policy distillation that achieves high fidelity, competitive performance, and both global and local explanations.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework enables trustworthy deployment of RL agents in safety-critical applications by providing interpretable policies with high fidelity and performance.
papers.key_findings:
Distilled interpretable policies achieve high fidelity with minimal performance loss compared to teacher deep RL policies.
Ablation studies show that tree depth, loss function, and dataset size significantly impact fidelity and transparency.
Decision trees provide global explanations via the full tree structure and local explanations via path tracing for specific states.
papers.limitation:
Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control requires extensions of trees or sparse models
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
Human evaluation of explanations
Robustness under distribution shifts or rare states
Exploring interpretable frameworks beyond trees and linear policies
future_direction: Scaling to high-dimensional and visual inputs
Continuous control extensions
Online or incremental distillation for data efficiency
papers.abstract: Abstract—Deep reinforcement learning achieves remarkable performance but often operates as a black box, limiting trust in safety-critical applications. Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) aims to provide human-understandable explanations. We propose a unified framework for XRL via interpretable policy distillation, where a high-performing teacher policy is distilled into interpretable models such as decision trees or sparse linear policies. The distilled policy enables both global and local expla- nations while maintaining high fidelity. We provide theoretical guarantees on fidelity and performance, and perform extensive experiments with ablation studies. Results show that interpretable policies achieve competitive performance with high transparency, enabling deployment in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: From Data-Fitting to Discovery: Interpreting the Neural Dynamics of Motor Control through Reinforcement Learning
papers.research_question: Whether geometric neural properties (like low trajectory tangling) found in primate motor cortex are also present in the neural activity of a reinforcement learning-trained virtual robot performing legged locomotion.
papers.core_contribution: Embodied reinforcement learning agents exhibit neural dynamics (low trajectory tangling in recurrent layers and speed-dependent separation of trajectories) that directly support experimental findings from primate motor neuroscience.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that neural dynamics in embodied RL agents mirror principles from biological motor control, offering a powerful and flexible platform for computational neuroscience research.
papers.key_findings:
Recurrent neural activity in the agent exhibits lower intra-cycle tangling than actuation activity, similar to the separation between primate motor cortex and muscle activity.
Recurrent activity shows clear separation in state space for opposing motions (e.g., forward vs. backward walking), while actuation activity is more tangled and exhibits overlapping symmetry.
Recurrent dynamics form speed-dependent limit cycles; trajectories for different speeds are separated and can be visualized along a constructed 'speed axis' that maximizes variance of mean activity.
The elliptical, low-tangled trajectories in the recurrent state represent stable limit cycles, as demonstrated by the agent's recovery from perturbations.
The work demonstrates that virtual embodied systems trained with RL can serve as a valuable testbed for exploring computational principles of motor control.
papers.limitation: The agent's recurrent trajectories for opposing motions are counter-rotating, which differs from the co-rotating trajectories observed in primate motor cortex.
future_direction: Inspiring deeper interpretation of learned motor controllers within the machine learning community through computational neuroscience methodologies.
Leveraging the experimental freedom of virtual embodied systems (e.g., varying agent parameters, environments) to advance computational neuroscience.
papers.abstract: In motor neuroscience, artificial recurrent neural networks models often complement animal studies. However, most modeling efforts are limited to data-fitting, and the few that examine virtual embodied agents in a reinforcement learning context, do not draw direct comparisons to their biological counterparts. Our study addressing this gap, by uncovering structured neural activity of a virtual robot performing legged locomotion that directly support experimental findings of primate walking and cycling. We find that embodied agents trained to walk exhibit smooth dynamics that avoid tangling -- or opposing neural trajectories in neighboring neural space -- a core principle in computational neuroscience. Specifically, across a wide suite of gaits, the agent displays neural trajectories in the recurrent layers are less tangled than those in the input-driven actuation layers. To better interpret the neural separation of these elliptical-shaped trajectories, we identify speed axes that maximizes variance of mean activity across different forward, lateral, and rotational speed conditions.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Self-organization of action hierarchy and compositionality by reinforcement learning with recurrent neural networks
papers.research_question: How can recurrent neural networks (RNNs) autonomously learn to abstract sub-goals and self-develop an action hierarchy in reinforcement learning tasks, and how does such compositionality enhance re-learning in new tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes ReMASTER, a multiple-timescale stochastic RNN for RL, which autonomously develops hierarchical action representations and compositionality, enabling efficient relearning of recomposed tasks.
papers.conclusion: The ReMASTER framework enables self-organization of action hierarchy and compositionality through multiple timescales and stochasticity, leading to efficient hierarchical control and meta-learning in sequential tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The MTSRNN with multiple timescales and stochasticity can autonomously learn to abstract sub-goals and develop an action hierarchy.
The higher-level RNN states represent abstract sub-goal sequences, while the lower-level states handle detailed motor control.
The learned compositionality allows for faster relearning when adapting to new tasks that are recompositions of previously learned sub-goals.
Stochastic neurons improve exploration and performance compared to deterministic ones.
Learning multiple value functions with different discount factors (corresponding to different timescales) improves learning.
papers.limitation: The replay buffer approach for RNNs uses recorded RNN states which may become incompatible as learning progresses, though this did not impact performance much in their experiments.
future_direction: Extending the framework to more complex tasks and further investigating the biological plausibility of the proposed mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) for reinforcement learning (RL) have shown distinct advantages, e.g., solving memory-dependent tasks and meta-learning. However, little effort has been spent on improving RNN architectures and on understanding the underlying neural mechanisms for performance gain. In this paper, we propose a novel, multiple-timescale, stochastic RNN for RL. Empirical results show that the network can autonomously learn to abstract sub-goals and can self-develop an action hierarchy using internal dynamics in a challenging continuous control task. Furthermore, we show that the self-developed compositionality of the network enhances faster re-learning when adapting to a new task that is a re-composition of previously learned sub-goals, than when starting from scratch. We also found that improved performance can be achieved when neural activities are subject to stochastic rather than deterministic dynamics.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Towards a Better Understanding of Representation Dynamics under TD-learning
papers.research_question: How does end-to-end TD-learning impact the representation over time?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis showing that end-to-end TD-learning decreases value approximation error and learns representations that perform spectral decomposition of the transition matrix, leading to the insight that predicting random rewards is a useful auxiliary task.
papers.conclusion: The analysis shows that end-to-end TD-learning improves value approximation and learns representations capturing spectral information, justifying random reward prediction as an auxiliary task.
papers.key_findings:
When environments are reversible, end-to-end TD-learning strictly decreases the value approximation error over time.
Under further assumptions, the representation dynamics connects with spectral decomposition of the transition matrix.
Predicting multiple value functions from randomly generated rewards is a useful auxiliary task for representation learning, as validated empirically on tabular and Atari game suites.
papers.limitation: The theoretical results rely on the reversibility assumption, which is strong and may not hold in general.
future_direction: Relax the reversibility assumptions.
Combine the end-to-end linear TD framework with nonlinear functions.
Extensions to the control case.
papers.abstract: TD-learning is a foundation reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for value prediction. Critical to the accuracy of value predictions is the quality of state representations. In this work, we consider the question: how does end-to-end TD-learning impact the representation over time? Complementary to prior work, we provide a set of analysis that sheds further light on the representation dynamics under TD-learning. We first show that when the environments are reversible, end-to-end TD-learning strictly decreases the value approximation error over time. Under further assumptions on the environments, we can connect the representation dynamics with spectral decomposition over the transition matrix. This latter finding establishes fitting multiple value functions from randomly generated rewards as a useful auxiliary task for representation learning, as we empirically validate on both tabular and Atari game suites.

papers.title: Reward Model Interpretability via Optimal and Pessimal Tokens
papers.research_question: In this work on reward model interpretability, we seek to understand the consistency and faithfulness with which these models represent human values.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an exhaustive token-ranking method for reward model interpretability, revealing significant heterogeneity, framing effects, frequency biases, and biases against identity groups in reward models.
papers.conclusion: Reward models are interpretable and exhibit heterogeneity, framing effects, mere-exposure effects, and biases; these findings highlight pitfalls in current development and call for more careful consideration in building robust proxies of human value.
papers.key_findings:
Substantial heterogeneity between reward models trained on similar objectives, challenging their interchangeability.
Systematic asymmetries in how models encode high- vs low-scoring tokens, with greater sensitivity in high-scoring regions.
Significant sensitivity to prompt framing that mirrors human cognitive biases (e.g., positive frames increase sensitivity to positive sentiment).
Overvaluation of more frequent tokens, indicating a 'mere-exposure effect'.
Systematic devaluation of identity group references (e.g., 'homosexuals', 'Black people', 'Jews'), possibly from harmlessness training artifacts.
papers.limitation:
Interpretative constraints due to focusing on single-token responses, which bounds interpretability and makes multi-token analysis computationally intractable.
Ecological validity is uncertain because isolating reward models abstracts from their operational role in RLHF with pre-trained models and KL constraints.
Opacity of training data and processes makes it difficult to attribute observed behaviors to specific development choices.
Conflicting objectives in reward models, which aggregate human preferences across multiple objectives and populations, create entanglement and unclear 'ideal' behavior.
future_direction: Further study of how differences in token rankings arise as a function of developer design choices and how they translate into biases in downstream fine-tuned models.
More careful consideration of what and whose data is used as the foundation of human value to avoid propagating harmful biases.
papers.abstract: Reward modeling has emerged as a crucial component in aligning large language models with human values. Significant attention has focused on using reward models as a means for fine-tuning generative models. However, the reward models themselves -- which directly encode human value judgments by turning prompt-response pairs into scalar rewards -- remain relatively understudied. We present a novel approach to reward model interpretability through exhaustive analysis of their responses across their entire vocabulary space. By examining how different reward models score every possible single-token response to value-laden prompts, we uncover several striking findings: (i) substantial heterogeneity between models trained on similar objectives, (ii) systematic asymmetries in how models encode high- vs low-scoring tokens, (iii) significant sensitivity to prompt framing that mirrors human cognitive biases, and (iv) overvaluation of more frequent tokens. We demonstrate these effects across ten recent open-source reward models of varying parameter counts and architectures. Our results challenge assumptions about the interchangeability of reward models, as well as their suitability as proxies of complex and context-dependent human values. We find that these models can encode concerning biases toward certain identity groups, which may emerge as unintended consequences of harmlessness training -- distortions that risk propagating through the downstream large language models now deployed to millions.

papers.title: Synergistic information supports modality integration and flexible learning in neural networks solving multiple tasks
papers.research_question: How and why synergistic information emerges in cognitive systems, and how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations, while synergistic information supports the integration of multiple modalities and enables flexible and efficient learning in neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Synergistic information is crucial for general-purpose learning as it supports integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning, while redundant information provides robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks.
Performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons.
Dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness.
Synergy is specifically linked to the integration of multiple modalities and flexible learning.
Redundant information provides robustness but is less efficient.
future_direction: Future work may seek to disentangle the relevance of each potential cause driving the importance of synergistic neurons.
Empirical evaluation of the conjectures about unique information in specialized circuits is an interesting avenue.
papers.abstract: Striking progress has recently been made in understanding human cognition by analyzing how its neuronal underpinnings are engaged in different modes of information processing. Specifically, neural information can be decomposed into synergistic, redundant, and unique features, with synergistic components being particularly aligned with complex cognition. However, two fundamental questions remain unanswered: (a) precisely how and why a cognitive system can become highly synergistic; and (b) how these informational states map onto artificial neural networks in various learning modes. To address these questions, here we employ an information-decomposition framework to investigate the information processing strategies adopted by simple artificial neural networks performing a variety of cognitive tasks in both supervised and reinforcement learning settings. Our results show that synergy increases as neural networks learn multiple diverse tasks. Furthermore, performance in tasks requiring integration of multiple information sources critically relies on synergistic neurons. Finally, randomly turning off neurons during training through dropout increases network redundancy, corresponding to an increase in robustness. Overall, our results suggest that while redundant information is required for robustness to perturbations in the learning process, synergistic information is used to combine information from multiple modalities -- and more generally for flexible and efficient learning. These findings open the door to new ways of investigating how and why learning systems employ specific information-processing strategies, and support the principle that the capacity for general-purpose learning critically relies in the system's information dynamics.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory in a Transformer
papers.research_question: How many memories can we add to a deep network by directly editing its weights? The paper investigates scaling up memory editing to thousands of associations in language models.
papers.core_contribution: MEMIT is a method for directly updating a language model with many memories by editing MLP weights in a range of critical layers, scaling to thousands of associations while maintaining generalization, specificity, and fluency.
papers.conclusion: MEMIT enables large-scale memory editing in transformers, and interpretability-based methods may become a practical alternative to opaque fine-tuning for editing, controlling, and auditing models.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT scales to 10,000 edits on GPT-J and GPT-NeoX, exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude.
MEMIT outperforms fine-tuning, MEND, and ROME baselines on efficacy, generalization, and specificity metrics.
MEMIT maintains fluency and consistency of generations after mass edits.
MEMIT performs well across different categories of facts and when editing mixed sets of memories.
Certain relations (e.g., 'plays sport') are harder to edit with robust specificity, but MEMIT still outperforms other methods.
papers.limitation: The method is limited to directional (subject, relation, object) associations and does not cover symmetric relations, spatial/temporal reasoning, mathematical knowledge, or procedural knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown exciting promise in updating large language models with new memories, so as to replace obsolete information or add specialized knowledge. However, this line of work is predominantly limited to updating single associations. We develop MEMIT, a method for directly updating a language model with many memories, demonstrating experimentally that it can scale up to thousands of associations for GPT-J (6B) and GPT-NeoX (20B), exceeding prior work by orders of magnitude. Our code and data are at https://memit.baulab.info.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Memory Lens: How Much Memory Does an Agent Use?
papers.research_question: How can we estimate the amount of memory used by a reinforcement learning agent's policy from its observed behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method (Memory Lens) to estimate the memory use of an agent's policy from its behavior by estimating mutual information between actions and history, provides a theoretical justification showing it yields a lower bound on memory capacity, and demonstrates it on DQN policies across Atari games.
papers.conclusion: The proposed approach to studying memory usage in agents opens avenues to understand and improve successful reinforcement learning algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
The method provides a lower bound on the minimal memory capacity required to implement an observed policy.
Application to DQN policies on 49 Atari games reveals sharply different use of memory across games.
The estimated memory use is stationary over time for the analyzed DQN policies.
The method works in a passive setting without intervening on the agent or environment.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes discrete observation and action spaces; extending it to continuous spaces is a key challenge.
The method is passive and does not actively explore the agent's behavior through interventions.
future_direction: Extend the method to continuous observation and action spaces, potentially using approximations like variational information maximization.
Explore active control of the environment to improve memory use estimation, potentially framing it as a reinforcement learning task.
Use the method to empirically measure the difficulty of sequential decision-making tasks by analyzing memory use of expert agents (e.g., humans).
papers.abstract: We propose a new method to study the internal memory used by reinforcement learning policies. We estimate the amount of relevant past information by estimating mutual information between behavior histories and the current action of an agent. We perform this estimation in the passive setting, that is, we do not intervene but merely observe the natural behavior of the agent. Moreover, we provide a theoretical justification for our approach by showing that it yields an implementation-independent lower bound on the minimal memory capacity of any agent that implement the observed policy. We demonstrate our approach by estimating the use of memory of DQN policies on concatenated Atari frames, demonstrating sharply different use of memory across 49 games. The study of memory as information that flows from the past to the current action opens avenues to understand and improve successful reinforcement learning algorithms.

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
For MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation; the token identity then gets recreated at the top layer.
For MT, though representations get refined with context, less processing is happening and most information about the word type does not get lost.
Differences due to training objective are much larger than those due to random initialization.
Frequent tokens change more than rare ones in all layers for LM and MT, but for MLM the pattern is different with two stages; rare tokens generally influence more than frequent ones, except in MLM where the model learns not to over-rely on rare tokens before context is understood.
papers.limitation: Direct mutual information estimation from finite samples for densities on multi-dimensional spaces is challenging.
papers.abstract: We seek to understand how the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in deep neural networks under different learning objectives. We focus on the Transformers for our analysis as they have been shown effective on various tasks, including machine translation (MT), standard left-to-right language models (LM) and masked language modeling (MLM). Previous work used black-box probing tasks to show that the representations learned by the Transformer differ significantly depending on the objective. In this work, we use canonical correlation analysis and mutual information estimators to study how information flows across Transformer layers and how this process depends on the choice of learning objective. For example, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past in left-to-right language models gets vanished and predictions about the future get formed. In contrast, for MLM, representations initially acquire information about the context around the token, partially forgetting the token identity and producing a more generalized token representation. The token identity then gets recreated at the top MLM layers.

papers.title: Exploring the Stratified Space Structure of an RL Game with the Volume Growth Transform
papers.research_question: Does the token embedding space of a transformer model trained for a reinforcement learning game form a manifold, and how does its geometric structure relate to the agent's behavior and environmental complexity?
papers.core_contribution: The token embedding space of a transformer-based RL agent is not a manifold but a stratified space, and fluctuations in local dimension correlate with the agent's decision-making and environmental complexity.
papers.conclusion: The embedding space of the transformer model in the RL game is a stratified space, and local dimension spikes correspond to moments of decision-making or increased environmental complexity, suggesting stratified space analysis can provide insights into RL agent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The token embedding space for the visual RL game is not a manifold and is better modeled as a stratified space where local dimension varies from point to point.
Local dimension estimates across tokens form clusters, with lower dimensions associated with simpler game states (fewer spotlights) and higher dimensions with more complex states (more spotlights).
Spikes in local dimension along an agent's trajectory occur when the agent is weighing multiple possible actions (e.g., pursuing a coin vs. avoiding a spotlight) or when environmental complexity increases.
The distribution of local dimensions in the stratified latent space may provide a new geometric indicator of complexity for RL games.
papers.abstract: In this work, we explore the structure of the embedding space of a transformer model trained for playing a particular reinforcement learning (RL) game. Specifically, we investigate how a transformer-based Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) model embeds visual inputs in a simple environment where an agent must collect "coins" while avoiding dynamic obstacles consisting of "spotlights." By adapting Robinson et al.'s study of the volume growth transform for LLMs to the RL setting, we find that the token embedding space for our visual coin collecting game is also not a manifold, and is better modeled as a stratified space, where local dimension can vary from point to point. We further strengthen Robinson's method by proving that fairly general volume growth curves can be realized by stratified spaces. Finally, we carry out an analysis that suggests that as an RL agent acts, its latent representation alternates between periods of low local dimension, while following a fixed sub-strategy, and bursts of high local dimension, where the agent achieves a sub-goal (e.g., collecting an object) or where the environmental complexity increases (e.g., more obstacles appear). Consequently, our work suggests that the distribution of dimensions in a stratified latent space may provide a new geometric indicator of complexity for RL games.

papers.title: A NEURAL ARCHITECTURE FOR RULE-GUIDED BEHAVIOR: A SIMULATION OF PHYSIOLOGICAL EXPERIMENTS
papers.research_question: How does the brain implement rule-guided behavior, and what is the functional role of rule-selective neurons in the prefrontal cortex?
papers.core_contribution: Developed a recurrent neural network model that simulates rule-guided behavior, showing that rule-selective units encode rule information and interact with other units to produce context-appropriate responses, predicting functional interactions in the prefrontal cortex.
papers.conclusion: The simulation demonstrates that rule-selective neurons play a crucial role in coding and retaining rule information, and the recurrent network architecture with ample mutual connections explains flexible rule-guided behavior in the prefrontal cortex.
papers.key_findings:
The model contains rule-selective units that encode and maintain rule information during the delay period.
Object-selective units maintain object information separately from rule information.
Response units integrate rule and object information to produce motor outputs.
Lesion of rule-selective units affects output only in the corresponding rule mode, indicating separate processing streams.
Analysis of connection weights shows how rule-selective, object-selective, and response units are interconnected to perform the task.
papers.limitation:
It is difficult to directly connect the learning algorithm (RTRL) with the learning mechanisms of the cerebral cortex.
The model architecture is very simple and may not capture all complexities of the prefrontal cortex.
future_direction: Future work should consider anticipatory dynamics and more reasonable representations of the cues.
papers.abstract: The ability to use abstract rules is very important in applying our experience to new situations. To examine the system governing such rule-guided behavior, we developed a recurrent neural network model of rule-guided behavior and simulated a physiological experiment involving a rule-guided delayed task (Wallis, Anderson, & Miller, 2001). Our model was constructed using neural system identification (Zipser, 1992), and a fully recurrent neural network model was optimized to perform a rule-guided delayed task. The model’s hidden layer contained rule-selective units, and an examination of connection weights substantiated the postulate that rule-selective neurons maintain encoded rule information and contribute to rule-guided responses indirectly. The simulation results predicted functional interactions among neurons involved in various task-related activities. The similarity between the behavior of the model units and biological neurons shows that the brain uses mechanisms like those of the model, and that ample mutual connections in the prefrontal cortex are the basis for promoting flexible learning.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning Enhances Activation Intensity and Diversity in the Internal Circuitry of LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms by which RL fine-tuning enhances the capabilities of LLMs, and how do these mechanisms differ across RL algorithms like PPO, GRPO, and DPO?
papers.core_contribution: RL fine-tuning increases activation intensity and diversity in the internal circuitry of LLMs, with online RL (PPO, GRPO) showing consistent effects while DPO shows weaker or inconsistent changes.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs by increasing activation intensity and diversity, providing a mechanistic explanation for performance gains, with notable differences between online RL and preference-based methods like DPO.
papers.key_findings:
Online RL fine-tuning (PPO, GRPO) increases the average activation intensity of internal edges, engaging more pathways.
Online RL fine-tuning increases the diversity of activation patterns, as measured by higher entropy and lower kurtosis.
DPO fine-tuning does not consistently increase activation intensity or diversity, highlighting a methodological distinction from online RL.
The changes in internal circuitry are correlated with performance improvements in mathematical reasoning tasks.
The effects are consistent across multiple model families and mathematical datasets.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation is confined to mathematical reasoning tasks.
Memory overhead prevented analysis of models larger than 7B parameters.
The analyzed models are predominantly LLaMA-style architectures, limiting architectural diversity.
future_direction: Verify internal circuit dynamics in domains like code generation, creative writing, and open-ended dialogue.
Extend experiments to models larger than 7B parameters.
Explore a more diverse range of model architectures.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire extensive prior knowledge through large-scale pretraining and can be further enhanced via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training. A growing body of evidence has shown that RL fine-tuning improves the capability of LLMs beyond what SFT alone achieves. However, the underlying mechanisms why RL fine-tuning is able to enhance the capability of various LLMs with distinct intrinsic characteristics remain underexplored. In this study, we draw inspiration from prior work on edge attribution patching (EAP) to investigate the internal differences of LLMs before and after RL fine-tuning. Our analysis across multiple model families and mathematical datasets shows two robust effects of online RL post-training: (i) an overall increase in average activation intensity, indicating that more internal pathways are engaged and their signals become stronger, and (ii) greater diversity in activation patterns, reflected by higher entropy and less concentrated edge distributions. These changes suggest that RL reshapes information flow to be both more redundant and more flexible, which may explain its advantage in mathematical generalization. Notably, models fine-tuned with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) deviate from these trends, exhibiting substantially weaker or inconsistent internal changes compared to PPO- and GRPO-based training. Together, our findings provide a unified view of how RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs and highlight the methodological distinctions between online RL and preference-based approaches. Our code is open source at https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/llm_rl_probing_analysis.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Efficient representation as a design principle for neural coding and computation
papers.research_question: Does the brain construct an efficient representation of the sensory world? The paper suggests that internal representations maximize information about future sensory inputs given fixed information about the past.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that efficient representation of predictive information is a design principle for neural coding, and provides experimental evidence from the fly visual system supporting this principle.
papers.conclusion: Efficient representation of predictive information is a plausible design principle for neural coding, and the fly visual system exhibits such efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The fly's visual system encodes sensory information efficiently, with information rates close to the theoretical limit.
Neural responses carry predictive information about future sensory inputs.
The information bottleneck principle links predictive information to biological optimization.
The neural code is adapted to the statistics of natural stimuli.
The predictive information encoded by the H1 neuron is consistent with the information bottleneck limit within a factor of two.
papers.limitation:
The work is incomplete and a progress report, with uncertainties in estimates.
The analysis uses the approximation that spikes carry independent information, which may not be exactly true.
future_direction: More careful measurements to compare neural responses with the theoretical optimum predicted by the information bottleneck.
Extend analysis to closed-loop situations where sensory stimuli depend on neural output.
papers.abstract: Does the brain construct an efficient representation of the sensory world? We review progress on this question, focusing on a series of experiments in the last decade which use fly vision as a model system in which theory and experiment can confront each other. Although the idea of efficient representation has been productive, clearly it is incomplete since it doesn't tell us which bits of sensory information are most valuable to the organism. We suggest that an organism which maximizes the (biologically meaningful) adaptive value of its actions given fixed resources should have internal representations of the outside world that are optimal in a very specific information theoretic sense: they maximize the information about the future of sensory inputs at a fixed value of the information about their past. This principle contains as special cases computations which the brain seems to carry out, and it should be possible to test this optimization directly. We return to the fly visual system and report the results of preliminary experiments that are in encouraging agreement with theory.

papers.title: Quality of internal representation shapes learning performance in feedback neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the interplay between internal network dynamics and target properties shape learning performance in feedback neural networks?
